los.text: Describe the main causes, signs and symptoms and pathophysiology of hypovolaemia
los.html:
HypovolaemiaReduced circulating (intravascular) volume.
Causes
  • Haemorrhage (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured AAA, ectopic, post-partum)
  • GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, fistulae, NG drainage)
  • Renal losses (diuretics, osmotic diuresis in DKA/HHS, Addison's, diabetes insipidus)
  • Skin (burns, heat, sweating)
  • Third-space losses (pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, sepsis capillary leak, ascites)
  • Poor intake (elderly, dysphagia).
Pathophysiology
  • ↓ venous return
  • → ↓ preload
  • → ↓ SV and CO
  • → ↓ BP
  • → baroreceptors
  • → sympathetic activation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction → cool pale peripheries), RAAS and ADH (Na⁺/water retention → oliguria, thirst), fluid shift from interstitium into vessels.
  • Decompensation → ↓ tissue perfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acidosis, organ failure (AKI, confusion).
SymptomsThirst, dizziness (especially on standing), fatigue, reduced urine output.
Signs
  • Tachycardia (earliest)
  • Prolonged capillary refill (>2 s)
  • Cool peripheries
  • Postural hypotension
  • Dry mucous membranes
  • ↓ skin turgor
  • Sunken eyes
  • ↓ JVP
  • Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h)
  • Tachypnoea
  • Confusion
  • Hypotension is a late sign (young people compensate until ~30% loss).
Haemorrhage class (ATLS)Blood lossHRBPMental state
I<15% (<750 mL)NormalNormalSlightly anxious
II15–30%>100Normal (↓ pulse pressure)Anxious
III30–40%>120↓Confused
IV>40%>140↓↓Lethargic

los.text: Describe the principles of treatment and management of hypovolaemia
sessions: Clin 2: Investigations, diagnosis and treatment of hypovolaemia
los.html:
ABCDE
  • High-flow O₂
  • 2 large-bore IV cannulae (14–16G)
  • Bloods (FBC, U&E, lactate, VBG, group and crossmatch, clotting, glucose)
  • Monitoring (HR, BP, sats, urine output via catheter)
  • Fluid balance chart.
Fluid resuscitation (NICE CG174)
  • 500 mL crystalloid bolus (0.9% NaCl or Hartmann's/balanced) over <15 min, reassess, repeat up to 2000 mL
  • Seek senior help if still shocked.
  • Smaller boluses (250 mL) if HF/elderly.
Haemorrhage
  • Stop the bleeding (pressure, tourniquet, pelvic binder, surgery, endoscopy, interventional radiology)
  • Blood products early (major haemorrhage protocol: RBC:FFP:platelets ~1:1:1)
  • Tranexamic acid within 3 h of trauma
  • Permissive hypotension (target SBP ~80–90 until control, unless head injury)
  • Avoid the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy).
Treat causeAntiemetics, stop diuretics/antihypertensives, insulin for DKA, steroids for adrenal crisis.
Monitor responseHR, BP, CRT, urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/h), lactate clearance, mental state; avoid fluid overload (crackles, ↑ JVP, oedema).
DiagnosisClinical assessment + response to fluid challenge; passive leg raise; in ICU: dynamic measures (pulse pressure variation, echo).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of fluid preparations and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
sessions: Clin 3: Principles of IV fluid administration
los.html:
FluidContents (mmol/L)Use
0.9% sodium chlorideNa⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154Resuscitation, replacement; large volumes → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
Hartmann's / Plasma-Lyte (balanced)Na⁺ ~131, K⁺ 5, Ca²⁺ 2, Cl⁻ 111, lactate 29Resuscitation, surgery; less acidosis (avoid in hyperkalaemia debated, liver failure)
5% glucose50 g/L glucose, no Na⁺Free water; distributes to all compartments (only ~1/12 stays intravascular); not for resuscitation
0.18% NaCl / 4% glucose (± KCl)Na⁺ 30Maintenance in adults; hyponatraemia risk (avoid in children)
Colloids (albumin, gelatins)Large moleculesAlbumin in specific cases (large-volume paracentesis, SBP); starches harmful (AKI)
Blood productsHaemorrhage
DistributionCrystalloids distribute across ECF → only ~¼ of 0.9% saline remains intravascular.
NICE "5 Rs"Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution, Reassessment.
Maintenance (adults)
  • 25–30 mL/kg/day water, ~1 mmol/kg/day Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻, 50–100 g/day glucose (to limit ketosis).
  • Reduce (20–25 mL/kg) in elderly, frail, renal/cardiac failure.
PotassiumAdd KCl to maintenance; max 10 mmol/h peripherally (unless ICU with cardiac monitoring); never as bolus.
PrescribeType, volume, rate; review daily with U&E, fluid balance, weight; oral route preferred when possible.

los.text: Explain the appropriate times to request U&Es and how to interpret the results
los.html:
• When to request U&Es: acutely unwell/admission
    • sepsis
    • dehydration/vomiting/diarrhoea
    • before and during IV fluids (daily)
    • starting/changing ACEi/ARB, diuretics, spironolactone (1–2 weeks after)
    • nephrotoxic drugs (gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs)
    • lithium/digoxin monitoring
    • CKD monitoring
    • pre-op
    • before contrast
    • AKI follow-up
    • arrhythmias.
ResultInterpretation
Na⁺ (135–145)Low: SIADH, diuretics, vomiting/diarrhoea, HF, cirrhosis, Addison's, hypotonic fluids. High: water loss/dehydration, DI
K⁺ (3.5–5.3)Low: diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, insulin, β2 agonists, Conn's. High: AKI/CKD, ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim, DKA, Addison's, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysed sample (check!)
Urea (2.5–7.8)↑ with dehydration, upper GI bleed (protein meal), high protein, catabolism, steroids; ↓ liver failure, malnutrition
Creatinine (60–110)Muscle mass dependent; ↑ in AKI/CKD; eGFR derived
Urea:creatinine ratioDisproportionately ↑ urea → pre-renal/dehydration or GI bleed
  • AKI (KDIGO): creatinine ↑ ≥26 μmol/L in 48 h or ≥1.5× baseline in 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
    • Compare with baseline.
K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes (peaked T, broad QRS) → IV calcium gluconate, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol; treat cause.

los.text: Describe the causes and pathogenesis of CKD and AKI
los.html:
AKI

Pre-renal(~70%; ↓ perfusion)Hypovolaemia, sepsis, HF, drugs (ACEi/NSAIDs/diuretics). Kidneys intact; urine concentrated, low urinary Na⁺. Reversible if perfusion restored; prolonged → ATN.
Intrinsic renal
  • Acute tubular necrosis (ischaemia, nephrotoxins: aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin) – commonest intrinsic
  • Glomerulonephritis (RPGN), acute interstitial nephritis (drugs: PPIs, NSAIDs, penicillins), vascular (vasculitis, HUS, malignant HTN).
Post-renal(obstruction)Stones, prostate enlargement, tumours, blocked catheter → ↑ tubular pressure → ↓ GFR. USS shows hydronephrosis.
ConsequencesFluid overload, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis), drug accumulation.

CKD

DefinitionAbnormal kidney structure/function >3 months: eGFR <60 and/or albuminuria (ACR ≥3 mg/mmol). Staged G1–G5 and A1–A3.
CausesDiabetic nephropathy (commonest), hypertension, glomerulonephritis (IgA), ADPKD, renovascular disease, chronic pyelonephritis/reflux, obstruction, drugs (lithium, NSAIDs).
Pathogenesis
  • Nephron loss
  • → hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons (↑ glomerular pressure, Ang II)
  • → proteinuria
  • → glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis
  • → progressive decline (common final pathway).
Complications
  • Renal anaemia (↓ EPO)
  • CKD-mineral bone disorder (↓ calcitriol, ↑ PO₄, ↑ PTH → secondary hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy)
  • Acidosis
  • Hyperkalaemia
  • Fluid overload
  • Hypertension
  • Cardiovascular disease (main cause of death)
  • Uraemia.
Management
  • BP control (ACEi/ARB if proteinuria)
  • SGLT2 inhibitor
  • Statin
  • Avoid nephrotoxins
  • Treat complications (EPO, phosphate binders, vitamin D)
  • Prepare for renal replacement therapy (dialysis, transplant) or conservative care.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology of shock and associated compensatory mechanisms (part 1)
los.html:
• Shock: circulatory failure → inadequate tissue O₂ delivery/use → cellular dysfunction.
    • Recognised by hypotension (MAP <65), tachycardia, ↑ lactate (>2), signs of hypoperfusion.
TypeMechanismExamplesHaemodynamics
Hypovolaemic↓ circulating volumeHaemorrhage, fluid loss, burns↓ preload, ↑ SVR, cold
CardiogenicPump failureMI, arrhythmias, myocarditis, valve rupture↓ CO, ↑ preload (↑ JVP), ↑ SVR, cold
ObstructiveObstruction to filling/outflowTension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE↓ CO, ↑ JVP
DistributiveVasodilationSepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic (spinal cord injury: bradycardia), adrenal crisis↓ SVR, often warm initially
Compensatory mechanisms
  • Neural: baroreceptor reflex → sympathetic activation (↑ HR, contractility, arteriolar and venous constriction → redistribution from skin, gut, kidneys to brain and heart).
  • Hormonal: adrenaline (adrenal medulla), RAAS (Ang II vasoconstriction, aldosterone Na⁺ retention), ADH (vasoconstriction + water retention), cortisol, glucagon (↑ glucose).
  • Fluid shift: ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → interstitial fluid moves into capillaries ("autotransfusion").
  • Respiratory: tachypnoea compensates for metabolic acidosis.
  • Renal: ↓ GFR, oliguria (conserves volume).
StagesCompensated → progressive (decompensation: acidosis, cell injury, ↑ capillary permeability) → irreversible (multi-organ failure).

los.text: Describe how the perception of cues and context influences the formation of health beliefs
los.html:
Health beliefsIndividuals' perceptions about illness, risk, causes, treatment and control, which drive health behaviour.
Formation through cues and context
  • Internal cues: symptoms (pain, fatigue), bodily sensations interpreted through prior experience and attention.
  • External cues: media campaigns, illness of friends/family, advice from clinicians, reminders (letters), social media, celebrity cases (e.g. "Jade Goody effect" on cervical screening).
  • Context: culture, religion, family, social networks, socioeconomic position, education, health literacy, previous healthcare experiences, trust.
Models
  • Health Belief Model: perceived susceptibility + perceived severity + perceived benefits − perceived barriers + cues to action + self-efficacy → behaviour.
  • Leventhal's Common-Sense Model (illness representations): identity, cause, timeline, consequences, control/cure → coping → appraisal.
  • Theory of Planned Behaviour: attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioural control → intention → behaviour.
  • Lay beliefs/lay epidemiology: "candidacy" (who gets heart attacks), Uncle Norman (smoked and lived to 90).
RelevanceExplore ICE; tailor information; anticipate barriers to adherence and screening uptake; placebo/nocebo effects; health promotion design.
